body.value:
This site is a Drupal site, and there is no Drupal running behind it.

Everything you're reading was rendered by Nuxt at build time, from a Drupal that existed for the length of that build and was then thrown away. The pages are static files on GitHub Pages. When I want to write something, a Drupal is started on demand, held open for as long as I need it, and destroyed again.

I've been building Fully Decoupled sites with Druxt for a few years now, and this is the furthest I've taken the idea so far...

Why bother

A small Drupal site spends almost all of its life idle, and all of its life being a server: patched, backed up, watched, and paid for. The only reason it has to be up is that a visitor might arrive, and Drupal is the thing that decides what a visitor sees.

That bill is why Drupal stopped being a hobbyist's tool. I learned Drupal on a shared host, on a site nobody was paying me for, and plenty of people I know came in the same way. You cannot do that now: a Drupal site is a server you are responsible for, and the ones cheap enough to play on are the ones running six months of unapplied security updates. So the people who would once have built a recipe site or a club site with Drupal build it somewhere else, and never find out what Drupal is good at.

A site that costs nothing to leave running, and asks for a server only while you are writing, is Drupal back within reach of that person. That is the part of this I actually care about.

Decoupling moves that decision to build time. Druxt reads Drupal over JSON:API and Nuxt renders the result to files, so what a visitor sees is decided once, when the site is built. After that, Drupal is only needed by the person writing.

That's the whole idea, and I don't think it's a new one. What's changed is that the tooling to make Drupal disposable is now good enough to lean on. Tome puts the content and configuration in the repository, and GitHub Actions will happily stand a Drupal up for twenty minutes and then throw it away.

How it fits together

  • Drupal, with its content and configuration committed to the repository by Tome. It gets installed from those files, used, and deleted.
  • Nuxt with Druxt, reading Drupal over JSON:API and building the static site.
  • GitHub Actions, which builds and deploys, and which will stand a Drupal up when somebody asks for one.

Nothing here is persistent except the repository. The database is created from committed files every time, which means the repository is the site: clone it and you have everything, content included.

Quickstart

The starter kit installs the frontend, Composer, and a local Drupal 11 on SQLite, straight from the committed config and content:

# Install and build the whole thing.
npx giget@1 gh:druxt/quickstart-druxt-serverless#develop my-site --install
cd my-site
npm run generate

You'll need PHP 8.3 or newer and Composer. The install provisions Drupal, starts it, and leaves you with a backend on 127.0.0.1:8888 and a static build in nuxt/dist.

My favourite part is what happens next. Stop Drupal, serve the build, and the site still works, because nothing it serves needed Drupal after the build finished:

# Drupal's job is done.
cd drupal && ./.devtools/stop
npx serve -s nuxt/dist

Deploying to Pages

The deploy workflow does what the install did, then publishes what it built. The Drupal it provisions exists only inside the job:

# .github/workflows/pages.yml
- name: Provision Drupal
  working-directory: drupal
  run: |
    .devtools/assemble
    .devtools/provision
    .devtools/start

- name: Generate the static site
  working-directory: nuxt
  env:
    ROUTER_BASE: /
    CONTENT_REPOSITORY: ${{ github.repository }}
  run: npm run generate

A user site at <name>.github.io serves from the domain root and doesn't need a base path. A project site does need ROUTER_BASE: /<repo>/, because a static build bakes its asset paths in and there's no server later to fix them up.

Editing it

This is the part I wasn't sure would work. Turn on Edit and every entity on the page gains a control. It's the frontend's own editing layer, not Drupal's, because the site is static and there's nothing to submit a form to.

Changes go into a cart. They're held in the browser, they survive a reload, and nothing is written until you say so. In the meantime the page keeps drawing itself with your changes in it, through the same components that render the published site. The article you're reading is the article you're editing. There's no editing view to translate back from.

Preview shows a change as the site will render it, in whichever view mode you ask for and at a real device width. The widths are real rather than a zoom, so the site's own media queries decide the layout. A page wider than the window gets scaled down to fit, and the scale is a control you can override.

Sending the work

There are two destinations, and they answer different questions.

Commit to backend sends the cart to a running Drupal over JSON:API, one request per resource, in dependency order. That's the short loop, and it validates against the site's real field definitions.

Open a pull request doesn't need a backend at all, and it's the one I use most. The cart becomes a document in a branch: the JSON:API resources, the bytes of any images, and an explicit list of deletions. A job on that pull request stands a Drupal up, applies the document through the entity API, and commits back the content Tome writes, so review sees the real content diff rather than a description of one.

Doing the conversion in Drupal is deliberate. Tome writes Drupal's own normalisation: references by target_uuid, an image's width and height read off the file, the processed body. Reproducing that in JavaScript would mean keeping a copy of Drupal's normalisers correct as Drupal changes under them, and that fails quietly. You'd get pull requests that review cleanly and break the next build.

Starting a backend

When I do want Drupal, a workflow starts one. It provisions the site, exposes it through a Cloudflare Quick Tunnel, publishes where it is, and holds it open:

# .github/workflows/authoring.yml
on:
  workflow_dispatch:
    inputs:
      minutes:
        description: 'How long to hold the backend open'
        default: '55'

workflow_dispatch is restricted to people with write access to the repository, and that's the access control the whole thing rests on. There's no other way to start a session, and no push, pull request or schedule can do it.

The session publishes its address to a branch and the frontend reads it. When the job ends the tunnel closes and the record is deleted, so there's nothing left running and nothing left to find.

What it costs you

Some things are worse this way, and I'd rather say so.

  • Publishing waits for a build. Content goes live when the site rebuilds, rather than when you press save. For a site that publishes a few times a week that's fine. For a newsroom it isn't.
  • Anything Drupal does per request is gone. Personalisation, forms that write on submit, anything that reads the current user. What's left is what can be decided at build time.
  • Starting a backend takes a few minutes. Provisioning Drupal from scratch isn't instant, and you wait for it.

What you get back is one repository that holds the whole site, and a maintenance job that begins and ends with a build. For a personal site or a small project site, I think that's a good trade.

The starter kit is at druxt/quickstart-druxt-serverless, and this site is at Decipher/Decipher.github.io. Both are open, so have a poke around.
